Sophistical Refutations Aristotle's treatise on apparent refutation: reasoning that seems genuine but is not, or is valid yet inappropriate to the subject, closed by a recapitulation and a sentence denying that anything of the inquiry existed before it.

definition What it treats

  • Subject "Sophistic refutations, i.e. what appear to be refutations but are really fallacies instead."1↘
    Sophistical Refutations is Aristotle's treatise on apparent refutation: per the translation of Pickard-Cambridge, it states its subject as "sophistic refutations, i.e. what appear to be refutations but are really fallacies instead".§1
  • Refutation Reasoning involving the contradictory of the given conclusion.1↘
    The treatise defines reasoning as resting on "certain statements such that they involve necessarily the assertion of something other than what has been stated, through what has been stated", and refutation as "reasoning involving the contradictory of the given conclusion".§2
  • Extended sense Includes reasoning that is valid but only appears appropriate to the thing in question.1↘
    It extends the definition: a sophistical refutation and syllogism is one that "appears to be valid but is not" and also one which, "though it is valid, only appears to be appropriate to the thing in question".§3
  • Sophist's art "The semblance of wisdom without the reality."1↘
    The art of the sophist is defined there as "the semblance of wisdom without the reality", and contentious arguments as those that reason or appear to reason from premisses that appear to be generally accepted but are not.§4

taxonomy Kinds of fallacy

  • Two styles Dependent on language, and independent of language.1↘
    The treatise states a two-fold division: "two styles of refutation: for some depend on the language used, while some are independent of language".§7
  • Six in language Ambiguity, amphiboly, combination, division of words, accent, form of expression.1↘
    Six depend on language, listed as "ambiguity, amphiboly, combination, division of words, accent, form of expression", and seven are independent of it.§8
  • Seven outside language Stated as seven kinds.1↘
    Six depend on language, listed as "ambiguity, amphiboly, combination, division of words, accent, form of expression", and seven are independent of it.§8
  • Why names Names are finite and things infinite, so one name carries several meanings.1↘
    Language is given its weight by a statement of the work: "the most prolific and usual domain is the argument that turns upon names only", because "names are finite and so is the sum-total of formulae, while things are infinite in number", so that a single name has a number of meanings.§9

practice Examination and sophistry

  • Examination A branch of dialectic.1↘
    The treatise distinguishes examination from sophistry: the art of examining is a branch of dialectic, while sophistic refutations, even when they prove the contradictory of a thesis, do not make clear whether the answerer is ignorant.§13
  • Dialectician and sophist The sophist only appears to apply the common principles to the matter in hand.1↘
    A dialectician is one who "regards the common principles with their application to the particular matter in hand", and one who only appears to do so is a sophist.§14
  • Krabbe's reading "A useful treatise for sophists", read in deposit 1697 against the article's sophistry opposition.1↘
    Krabbe, cited in deposit 1697, calls it "a useful treatise for sophists" who "should study fallacies not to avoid them, but rather to commit them when it suits their purposes"; the deposit finds the article's opposition between dialectic and sophistry in tension with that reading.§17

placement Place among the treatises

  • Appendix to the Topics Held as a field interpretation.1↘
    The treatise itself places demonstrative arguments in the Analytics and dialectic and examination arguments elsewhere, and a field source reads the work as "a final section, or an appendix, to the Topics", a reading it holds as interpretation.§5
  • Organon A grouping by the ancient commentators; the title was never Aristotle's.1↘
    The grouping of the work in an Organon is attributed by the same field source to "the ancient commentators", and that source adds that "Aristotle himself never uses this term".§6
  • Stylometry At the world pole on the first axis; the real text on the apparatus side after the file erratum.1↘
    Deposit 1585 reads the work stylometrically as a registry of what people do in argument, a candidate reading it states as a hypothesis, and deposits 1585 and 1586 place it at the world pole of the first axis, while a file erratum in 1586 puts the real text on the apparatus side.§19

ending The closing chapter

  • Aim A syllogistic capacity from endoxa, for dialectic and peirastic.2↘
    The work ends in chapter 34 with a recapitulation of the aim, in the Greek: "Προειλόμεθα μὲν οὖν εὑρεῖν δύναμίν τινα συλλογιστικὴν περὶ τοῦ προβληθέντος ἐκ τῶν ὑπαρχόντων ὡς ἐνδοξοτάτων".§20 The work of that capacity is given as dialectic's and the peirastic's: "τοῦτο γὰρ ἔργον ἐστὶ τῆς διαλεκτικῆς καθ᾿ αὑτὴν καὶ τῆς πειραστικῆς", and the text adds that sophistic's proximity shapes the discipline.§21
  • Socrates "Asked and did not answer"; on the archive's reading an antecedent source on neither reading.2↘
    The chapter holds that Socrates "asked and did not answer": "Σωκράτης ἠρώτα, ἀλλ᾿ οὐκ ἀπεκρίνετο· ὡμολόγει γὰρ οὐκ εἰδέναι".§23 Deposit 1603 reads this as either the artless examining everyone shares, from which nothing is received, or something the epilogue files under the inquiry's own purposes, and on neither reading as an antecedent source.§24
  • No predecessors "οὐδὲν παντελῶς ὑπῆρχεν", read literally in deposit 1603.2↘
    The chapter then states, in the Greek of 183b34-36: "Ταύτης δὲ τῆς πραγματείας οὐ τὸ μὲν ἦν τὸ δ᾿ οὐκ ἦν προεξειργασμένον, ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲν παντελῶς ὑπῆρχεν."§25 Deposit 1603 reads the sentence literally, as denying that anything of the inquiry existed beforehand, and holds that the closing chapter is built joint by joint so that the sentence can be kept.§27
  • Rhetoric and eristic Rhetoric grew by succession; paid teachers gave products, not the art.2↘
    The chapter divides discoveries by provenance: rhetoric advanced by succession, "Τισίας μὲν μετὰ τοὺς πρώτους, Θρασύμαχος δὲ μετὰ Τισίαν, Θεόδωρος δὲ μετὰ τοῦτον".§32 The paid teachers of eristic are likened to the instruction of Gorgias, and the text says they gave "οὐ γὰρ τέχνην ἀλλὰ τὰ ἀπὸ τῆς τέχνης", the products of the art and not the art.§33
  • Pioneering limit Omissions are to be forgiven and discoveries thanked.1↘
    The work closes by naming its own pioneering condition: "δεῖ δ᾿ ἡμᾶς μὴ λεληθέναι τὸ συμβεβηκὸς περὶ ταύτην τὴν πραγματείαν", and by asking its hearers for indulgence toward omissions and thanks for what has been found.§35

reception Reception

  • Gloss Translators render the sentence whole; the narrowing enters in the gloss.1↘
    Translators of the closing sentence render it whole, according to deposit 1603: the narrowing, to "no systematic treatment" or "no completed art", enters in the gloss.§36
  • Primacy The article's lead turns the total negation into the attribute "the first work to treat".1↘
    The article's lead states the work's priority as an attribute; deposit 1696 reads the sentence "about syllogizing we had absolutely nothing else earlier to say" as becoming "the first work to treat the subject of deductive reasoning", a total negation over a stated domain turned into a property, primacy.§41
  • Deleted particle A review series deleted οὐ at composition, reported as unperceived.2↘
    A blog record reports that across twenty rounds of simulated review, each round inserted a qualifier into the sentence, and that the terminal round endorsed a sentence that is Aristotle's with the particle οὐ removed.§39 The record reads this as the reception deleting the negation at composition, unperceived, as Sophistical Refutations 16 predicts, and as restoring provenance from others.§40
  • Faithful sentences Some article sentences stay faithful to their source.1↘
    The same deposit records that other sentences of the article stay faithful to their source, finding no attributization in them.§44

Sophistical Refutations (Greek: Σοφιστικοὶ Ἔλεγχοι, romanized: Sophistikoi Elenchoi; Latin: De Sophisticis Elenchis) is a text in Aristotle's Organon in which he identified twelve or thirteen fallacies.
According to Aristotle, this is the first work to treat the subject of deductive reasoning in ancient Greece (Soph. Ref., 34, 183b34 ff.).
In it, he attempts to develop a pattern of sound and genuine reasoning in opposition to the deceptive or misleading "art of sophistry".
On Sophistical Refutations consists of 34 chapters.
The book naturally falls in two parts: chapters concerned with tactics for the Questioner (3–8 and 12–15) and chapters concerned with tactics for the Answerer (16–32).
Besides, there is an introduction (1–2), an interlude (9–11), and a conclusion (33–34).
The fallacies Aristotle identifies in Chapter 4 (formal fallacies) and 5 (informal fallacies) of this book are the following:
Figure of speech or form of expression

Sophistical Refutations

Sophistical Refutations is Aristotle's treatise on apparent refutation: per the translation of Pickard-Cambridge, it states its subject as "sophistic refutations, i.e. what appear to be refutations but are really fallacies instead". The treatise defines reasoning as resting on "certain statements such that they involve necessarily the assertion of something other than what has been stated, through what has been stated", and refutation as "reasoning involving the contradictory of the given conclusion". It extends the definition: a sophistical refutation and syllogism is one that "appears to be valid but is not" and also one which, "though it is valid, only appears to be appropriate to the thing in question". The art of the sophist is defined there as "the semblance of wisdom without the reality", and contentious arguments as those that reason or appear to reason from premisses that appear to be generally accepted but are not. The treatise itself places demonstrative arguments in the Analytics and dialectic and examination arguments elsewhere, and a field source reads the work as "a final section, or an appendix, to the Topics", a reading it holds as interpretation. The grouping of the work in an Organon is attributed by the same field source to "the ancient commentators", and that source adds that "Aristotle himself never uses this term".

The treatise states a two-fold division: "two styles of refutation: for some depend on the language used, while some are independent of language". Six depend on language, listed as "ambiguity, amphiboly, combination, division of words, accent, form of expression", and seven are independent of it. Language is given its weight by a statement of the work: "the most prolific and usual domain is the argument that turns upon names only", because "names are finite and so is the sum-total of formulae, while things are infinite in number", so that a single name has a number of meanings. Its examples include the ambiguity of "learn" in "Those learn who know" and the accident fallacy of Coriscus, who if different from "man" would be "different from himself: for he is a man". Archive deposit 1697 reads the article's later Fallacies section as a conversion: its labels contradict its list, and a stated criterion becomes membership in a later taxonomy. That reading is paired in the deposit with the finding that the narrowing is unsound against the article's own sources, and the edit history records the section's labels as one editor's own reading of the text.

The treatise distinguishes examination from sophistry: the art of examining is a branch of dialectic, while sophistic refutations, even when they prove the contradictory of a thesis, do not make clear whether the answerer is ignorant. A dialectician is one who "regards the common principles with their application to the particular matter in hand", and one who only appears to do so is a sophist. The treatise says it is possible "to hold an examination on everything" by an art that "is not of the same kind as those which demonstrate". It lists five aims of contentious disputants, ending with reducing the opponent to babbling. Krabbe, cited in deposit 1697, calls it "a useful treatise for sophists" who "should study fallacies not to avoid them, but rather to commit them when it suits their purposes"; the deposit finds the article's opposition between dialectic and sophistry in tension with that reading. The same deposit reads the article's lead as substituting a truth-normative pattern for the endoxic capacity and as dropping the premisses, which are the programme's scope. Deposit 1585 reads the work stylometrically as a registry of what people do in argument, a candidate reading it states as a hypothesis, and deposits 1585 and 1586 place it at the world pole of the first axis, while a file erratum in 1586 puts the real text on the apparatus side.

The work ends in chapter 34 with a recapitulation of the aim, in the Greek: "Προειλόμεθα μὲν οὖν εὑρεῖν δύναμίν τινα συλλογιστικὴν περὶ τοῦ προβληθέντος ἐκ τῶν ὑπαρχόντων ὡς ἐνδοξοτάτων". The work of that capacity is given as dialectic's and the peirastic's: "τοῦτο γὰρ ἔργον ἐστὶ τῆς διαλεκτικῆς καθ᾿ αὑτὴν καὶ τῆς πειραστικῆς", and the text adds that sophistic's proximity shapes the discipline. Deposit 1697 reads the epilogue as an accounting of a capacity (δύναμις) for dialectic and peirastic. The chapter holds that Socrates "asked and did not answer": "Σωκράτης ἠρώτα, ἀλλ᾿ οὐκ ἀπεκρίνετο· ὡμολόγει γὰρ οὐκ εἰδέναι". Deposit 1603 reads this as either the artless examining everyone shares, from which nothing is received, or something the epilogue files under the inquiry's own purposes, and on neither reading as an antecedent source.

The chapter then states, in the Greek of 183b34-36: "Ταύτης δὲ τῆς πραγματείας οὐ τὸ μὲν ἦν τὸ δ᾿ οὐκ ἦν προεξειργασμένον, ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲν παντελῶς ὑπῆρχεν." It adds, of syllogizing: "περὶ δὲ τοῦ συλλογίζεσθαι παντελῶς οὐδὲν εἴχομεν πρότερον ἄλλο λέγειν, ἀλλ᾿ ἢ τριβῇ ζητοῦντες πολὺν χρόνον ἐπονοῦμεν". Deposit 1603 reads the sentence literally, as denying that anything of the inquiry existed beforehand, and holds that the closing chapter is built joint by joint so that the sentence can be kept. The deposit finds the transmission vocabulary, παρ᾽ ἑτέρων, ἐκ διαδοχῆς, ἐκ παραδόσεως, freshly used with three lines of names attached, and held in no instance of Socrates, and it reads the origination vocabulary ἐξ ὑπαρχῆς, ἐξ ἀρχῆς likewise. Deposit 1603 reads the ending as performing the peirastic operation on its reader: a reader who qualifies the sentence supplies what the text was written without, and does not perceive the supplying. The deposit disclaims any design: it does not claim the chapter was built as a trap, since structures do not need intentions to function. Deposit 1603 leaves Socrates' possession of the art where the chapter leaves it.

The chapter divides discoveries by provenance: rhetoric advanced by succession, "Τισίας μὲν μετὰ τοὺς πρώτους, Θρασύμαχος δὲ μετὰ Τισίαν, Θεόδωρος δὲ μετὰ τοῦτον". The paid teachers of eristic are likened to the instruction of Gorgias, and the text says they gave "οὐ γὰρ τέχνην ἀλλὰ τὰ ἀπὸ τῆς τέχνης", the products of the art and not the art. The text illustrates this with a shoemaker analogy: one who promised knowledge to spare the feet pain, and taught no shoemaking. The work closes by naming its own pioneering condition: "δεῖ δ᾿ ἡμᾶς μὴ λεληθέναι τὸ συμβεβηκὸς περὶ ταύτην τὴν πραγματείαν", and by asking its hearers for indulgence toward omissions and thanks for what has been found.

Translators of the closing sentence render it whole, according to deposit 1603: the narrowing, to "no systematic treatment" or "no completed art", enters in the gloss. Poste's note, as quoted in a blog catalogue record, finds it "difficult to reconcile Aristotle's assertion with what we know had been done by Plato and Socrates and the Eleatics and Megarians"; the record reads the premise as what we know and the sentence as what must be reconciled with it. The archive's tension with Prior Analytics I.31, where Aristotle calls division, practised throughout the Platonic dialogues, part of the inquiry, is stated in deposit 1576 and is read there as a tension and not as a refutation. A blog record reports that across twenty rounds of simulated review, each round inserted a qualifier into the sentence, and that the terminal round endorsed a sentence that is Aristotle's with the particle οὐ removed. The record reads this as the reception deleting the negation at composition, unperceived, as Sophistical Refutations 16 predicts, and as restoring provenance from others.

The article's lead states the work's priority as an attribute; deposit 1696 reads the sentence "about syllogizing we had absolutely nothing else earlier to say" as becoming "the first work to treat the subject of deductive reasoning", a total negation over a stated domain turned into a property, primacy. Deposit 1697 reads this conversion as the clearest of the article's changes, and records its edit history as the composition of two edits that ran opposite ways. On the same article, deposit 1697 finds the claim of exhaustiveness hedged by a footnote folded into the text, "Sometimes listed as twelve.", added in a 2025 edit. The same deposit records that other sentences of the article stay faithful to their source, finding no attributization in them. Deposit 1697 notes that no discussion of the lead, the gloss, the qualifier or the labels has ever taken place on the talk page.

Deposit 1576 states that the priority claim sits in tension with Prior Analytics I.31; deposit 1579 traces the edition of a received Socrates in the Second Letter into Aristotle's epilogue at SE 34 and leaves open whether such an edition implies anything about how many hands made the texts. Deposit 1587 holds that the two names Aristotle and Theophrastus fail as two authors and leaves the maker-count open.

Sophistical Refutations Aristotle's treatise on apparent refutation, with a division of fallacies into those dependent on language and those independent of it, closed by a claim that nothing preceded the inquiry.

definition What it treats

  • Subject Apparent refutations that are really fallacies.1↘
    Sophistical Refutations is Aristotle's treatise on apparent refutation: per Pickard-Cambridge, it states its subject as "sophistic refutations, i.e. what appear to be refutations but are really fallacies instead".§1
  • Sophist's art The semblance of wisdom without the reality.1↘
    It treats the sophist's art as "the semblance of wisdom without the reality".§3

taxonomy Kinds of fallacy

  • Six in language Ambiguity, amphiboly, combination, division, accent, form of expression.1↘
    It divides fallacies into six dependent on language and seven independent of it, and says names are the chief source because names are finite and things infinite.§4
  • Seven outside language Stated as seven kinds.1↘
    It divides fallacies into six dependent on language and seven independent of it, and says names are the chief source because names are finite and things infinite.§4

placement Place among the treatises

  • Appendix to the Topics A field interpretation.1↘
    The art of examining is a branch of dialectic, and a field source reads the work as an appendix to the Topics and places it in the Organon grouping of the ancient commentators.§5
  • Organon A grouping by the ancient commentators.1↘
    The art of examining is a branch of dialectic, and a field source reads the work as an appendix to the Topics and places it in the Organon grouping of the ancient commentators.§5

ending The closing chapter

  • Aim A syllogistic capacity from endoxa.1↘
    The work closes with a recapitulation of its aim, a syllogistic capacity from endoxa, with Socrates asking and not answering.§6
  • No predecessors "οὐδὲν παντελῶς ὑπῆρχεν".1↘
    Its last chapter states that of this inquiry "οὐδὲν παντελῶς ὑπῆρχεν", contrasts rhetoric's succession with paid teachers who gave products and not the art, and ends on its own pioneering limit.§7
  • Pioneering limit Omissions forgiven, discoveries thanked.1↘
    Its last chapter states that of this inquiry "οὐδὲν παντελῶς ὑπῆρχεν", contrasts rhetoric's succession with paid teachers who gave products and not the art, and ends on its own pioneering limit.§7

Expansion · The field's ontology — L_F(B)7 sentences · every one sourced below

Sophistical Refutations

Sophistical Refutations is Aristotle's treatise on apparent refutation: per Pickard-Cambridge, it states its subject as "sophistic refutations, i.e. what appear to be refutations but are really fallacies instead". The treatise defines reasoning and refutation, and extends the sophistical sense to reasoning that is valid but only appears appropriate to the thing in question. It treats the sophist's art as "the semblance of wisdom without the reality".

It divides fallacies into six dependent on language and seven independent of it, and says names are the chief source because names are finite and things infinite.

The art of examining is a branch of dialectic, and a field source reads the work as an appendix to the Topics and places it in the Organon grouping of the ancient commentators.

The work closes with a recapitulation of its aim, a syllogistic capacity from endoxa, with Socrates asking and not answering. Its last chapter states that of this inquiry "οὐδὲν παντελῶς ὑπῆρχεν", contrasts rhetoric's succession with paid teachers who gave products and not the art, and ends on its own pioneering limit.

Ethe two entities and their relationρ = constructs · witness case

E_A, the archive's entity: The archive's Sophistical Refutations is, centrally, its closing chapter (SE 34), whose sentence οὐδὲν παντελῶς ὑπῆρχεν (183b34-36) the archive reads literally: nothing of the inquiry existed beforehand. The chapter is built joint by joint so that the sentence can be kept; the transmission and origination vocabulary (παρ' ἑτέρων, ἐκ διαδοχῆς, ἐκ παραδόσεως, ἐξ ὑπαρχῆς) is supplied and never said of Socrates, who is named inside the inquiry's own purposes and not an antecedent source, and the ending performs the peirastic operation on its reader, who by qualifying the sentence supplies what the text lacks (SR1603-01 to SR1603-17, SRblog-24 to SRblog-26, SRblog-30). Translators render the sentence whole, and the qualification enters in the glosses (SR1603-03, SRblog-27 to SRblog-31). The reception layer deletes the negation at the point of composition, unperceived, as SE 16 predicts, and restores provenance from others (SR1574-10, SRblog-42 to SRblog-46). The archive's encyclopedia entry treats the Wikipedia article as an instance of this conversion: the total negation becomes the attribute of primacy (W2), the criterion-bearing taxonomy becomes membership in a later list (W7-W8), exhaustiveness is hedged (W1) and the endoxic capacity is replaced by a truth-normative pattern against sophistry (W3), while W4-W6 stay faithful (SR1696-05, SR1696-06, SR1697-04, SR1697-07 to SR1697-15). SE is also a stylometric object at the world pole of the first axis, with the registry-of-practice reading (SR1585-03, SR1585-06). It is the hinge of the archive's one-maker question: the priority claim sits in tension with Prior Analytics I.31 (SR1576-01), and the second-letter edition is traced into SE 34 (SR1579-21, SRblog-07). SR1603-01 SR1603-02 SR1603-03 SR1603-04 SR1603-06 SR1603-09 SR1603-12 SR1603-13 SR1603-15 SR1603-17 SRblog-24 SRblog-26 SRblog-30 SRblog-42 SRblog-43 SRblog-46 SR1574-10 SR1696-05 SR1697-04 SR1697-07 SR1697-13 SR1697-15 SR1585-03 SR1576-01 SR1579-21; defining papers #1603, #1574, #1697, #1696, #1576

E_F, the field's entity (type C — a conventional reading holds it (public entity: a work in Aristotle's Organon, the subject of an encyclopedia article)): The field holds Sophistical Refutations as Aristotle's treatise on apparent refutations: reasoning that seems genuine but is not, or is valid yet inappropriate to the subject (F1, F20). It rests on a two-fold division of fallacies into six language-dependent kinds (ambiguity, amphiboly, combination, division, accent, form of expression) and seven independent of language (F11, F12, F13), with names as the chief source of apparent refutation because names are finite and things infinite (F4, F5). The sophist's art is the semblance of wisdom without the reality (F6), and contentious argument reasons from apparently accepted premisses (F7). The work is the appendix or final section of the Topics (F38), belonging to the Organon grouping of the ancient commentators, a title Aristotle never used (F36, F37), with demonstrative argument treated in the Analytics (F8). It ends in chapter 33-34 with a recapitulation of the inquiry's aim, a syllogistic capacity from endoxa serving dialectic and peirastic (F42, F43), shaped by sophistic's proximity (F44), and with Socrates asking but not answering because he admitted not knowing (F46). It closes with the claim that nothing at all preceded the theory of syllogism and refutation (F64, F65), the pioneering status of the work (F71, F72) and the contrast with rhetoric's succession and the paid teachers who gave products rather than the art (F67-F70).

ρ = constructs: The archive reads the encyclopedia article's Sophistical Refutations as made by reception: the article's primacy claim, its list labels, its hedge and its sophistry opposition are not Aristotle's sentences but conversions of them, supplied by receiving texts (the discipline's glosses, the edit history, the models trained on both). The archive's own entity is the text's closing operation, which these receptions convert into attributes. This is the same attestation structure the archive reads in Plato Second Letter 314c, where the received character is made by what receives it. SRblog-30 SRblog-42 SRblog-46 SR1696-05 SR1696-06 SR1697-04 SR1697-07 SR1697-08 SR1697-11 SR1697-13 SR1697-19 SR1697-20 SR1697-21. Guard: ρ claims only that the archive treats the article's attributes as conversions supplied by reception, on the specific sentences W1, W2, W3, W7 and W8 and their stated edit histories. It does not claim that every field claim is a reception artefact, that the field's claims on definition, taxonomy and scope (F1-F31, F38) are wrong or absent from Aristotle, or that W4-W6 are converted (SR1697-15 records them as faithful). It does not claim the SE 34 reading is the only defensible one: the archive itself marks the maker-count question and Socrates' possession of the art as left open (SR1603-10, SR1579-24).

The case: the archive's ontology rules, the suppressed witness (v0.9). the readings disagree on ρ; the reading of ρ = constructs is taken (ruled 2026-10-25: "if the readings disagree go constructs"). The reading taken gave equal: The archive does not contest the field's ontology of the work. Both hold Sophistical Refutations as Aristotle's treatise on apparent refutation, the closing recapitulation, and the no-predecessor claim; the field itself carries the Greek of 183b34-36 (F64, F65) and the pioneering limit (F71, F72), so the field holds the ontology, even if the article's lead converts it. What the archive adds is the unqualified reading of the closing sentence, the transmission-vocabulary analysis, the enacted-peirastic reading, the conversion measurements on reception, and the stylometric and maker-count questions. Where the archive's literal reading meets the field's article lead (W2: 'the first work to treat'), the two compose within one claim space: W2's primacy is read as the received attribute and F64 as the underlying sentence. The law of the suppressed witness does not apply, because the field holds the ontology of the entity, though in part marginally through the Greek ledger rows and not through the article's prose.

Sophistical Refutations is Aristotle's treatise on apparent refutation: per Pickard-Cambridge, it states its subject as "sophistic refutations, i.e. what appear to be refutations but are really fallacies instead". The treatise defines reasoning and refutation, and extends the sophistical sense to reasoning that is valid but only appears appropriate to the thing in question. It treats the sophist's art as "the semblance of wisdom without the reality". It divides fallacies into six dependent on language and seven independent of it, and says names are the chief source because names are finite and things infinite. The art of examining is a branch of dialectic, and a field source reads the work as an appendix to the Topics and places it in the Organon grouping of the ancient commentators. The work closes with a recapitulation of its aim, a syllogistic capacity from endoxa, with Socrates asking and not answering. Its last chapter states that of this inquiry "οὐδὲν παντελῶς ὑπῆρχεν", contrasts rhetoric's succession with paid teachers who gave products and not the art, and ends on its own pioneering limit.

Sophistical Refutations is Aristotle's treatise on apparent refutation: per the translation of Pickard-Cambridge, it states its subject as "sophistic refutations, i.e. what appear to be refutations but are really fallacies instead". The treatise defines reasoning as resting on "certain statements such that they involve necessarily the assertion of something other than what has been stated, through what has been stated", and refutation as "reasoning involving the contradictory of the given conclusion". It extends the definition: a sophistical refutation and syllogism is one that "appears to be valid but is not" and also one which, "though it is valid, only appears to be appropriate to the thing in question". The art of the sophist is defined there as "the semblance of wisdom without the reality", and contentious arguments as those that reason or appear to reason from premisses that appear to be generally accepted but are not. The treatise itself places demonstrative arguments in the Analytics and dialectic and examination arguments elsewhere, and a field source reads the work as "a final section, or an appendix, to the Topics", a reading it holds as interpretation. The grouping of the work in an Organon is attributed by the same field source to "the ancient commentators", and that source adds that "Aristotle himself never uses this term". The treatise states a two-fold division: "two styles of refutation: for some depend on the language used, while some are independent of language". Six depend on language, listed as "ambiguity, amphiboly, combination, division of words, accent, form of expression", and seven are independent of it. Language is given its weight by a statement of the work: "the most prolific and usual domain is the argument that turns upon names only", because "names are finite and so is the sum-total of formulae, while things are infinite in number", so that a single name has a number of meanings. Its examples include the ambiguity of "learn" in "Those learn who know" and the accident fallacy of Coriscus, who if different from "man" would be "different from himself: for he is a man". Archive deposit 1697 reads the article's later Fallacies section as a conversion: its labels contradict its list, and a stated criterion becomes membership in a later taxonomy. That reading is paired in the deposit with the finding that the narrowing is unsound against the article's own sources, and the edit history records the section's labels as one editor's own reading of the text. The treatise distinguishes examination from sophistry: the art of examining is a branch of dialectic, while sophistic refutations, even when they prove the contradictory of a thesis, do not make clear whether the answerer is ignorant. A dialectician is one who "regards the common principles with their application to the particular matter in hand", and one who only appears to do so is a sophist. The treatise says it is possible "to hold an examination on everything" by an art that "is not of the same kind as those which demonstrate". It lists five aims of contentious disputants, ending with reducing the opponent to babbling. Krabbe, cited in deposit 1697, calls it "a useful treatise for sophists" who "should study fallacies not to avoid them, but rather to commit them when it suits their purposes"; the deposit finds the article's opposition between dialectic and sophistry in tension with that reading. The same deposit reads the article's lead as substituting a truth-normative pattern for the endoxic capacity and as dropping the premisses, which are the programme's scope. Deposit 1585 reads the work stylometrically as a registry of what people do in argument, a candidate reading it states as a hypothesis, and deposits 1585 and 1586 place it at the world pole of the first axis, while a file erratum in 1586 puts the real text on the apparatus side. The work ends in chapter 34 with a recapitulation of the aim, in the Greek: "Προειλόμεθα μὲν οὖν εὑρεῖν δύναμίν τινα συλλογιστικὴν περὶ τοῦ προβληθέντος ἐκ τῶν ὑπαρχόντων ὡς ἐνδοξοτάτων". The work of that capacity is given as dialectic's and the peirastic's: "τοῦτο γὰρ ἔργον ἐστὶ τῆς διαλεκτικῆς καθ᾿ αὑτὴν καὶ τῆς πειραστικῆς", and the text adds that sophistic's proximity shapes the discipline. Deposit 1697 reads the epilogue as an accounting of a capacity (δύναμις) for dialectic and peirastic. The chapter holds that Socrates "asked and did not answer": "Σωκράτης ἠρώτα, ἀλλ᾿ οὐκ ἀπεκρίνετο· ὡμολόγει γὰρ οὐκ εἰδέναι". Deposit 1603 reads this as either the artless examining everyone shares, from which nothing is received, or something the epilogue files under the inquiry's own purposes, and on neither reading as an antecedent source. The chapter then states, in the Greek of 183b34-36: "Ταύτης δὲ τῆς πραγματείας οὐ τὸ μὲν ἦν τὸ δ᾿ οὐκ ἦν προεξειργασμένον, ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲν παντελῶς ὑπῆρχεν." It adds, of syllogizing: "περὶ δὲ τοῦ συλλογίζεσθαι παντελῶς οὐδὲν εἴχομεν πρότερον ἄλλο λέγειν, ἀλλ᾿ ἢ τριβῇ ζητοῦντες πολὺν χρόνον ἐπονοῦμεν". Deposit 1603 reads the sentence literally, as denying that anything of the inquiry existed beforehand, and holds that the closing chapter is built joint by joint so that the sentence can be kept. The deposit finds the transmission vocabulary, παρ᾽ ἑτέρων, ἐκ διαδοχῆς, ἐκ παραδόσεως, freshly used with three lines of names attached, and held in no instance of Socrates, and it reads the origination vocabulary ἐξ ὑπαρχῆς, ἐξ ἀρχῆς likewise. Deposit 1603 reads the ending as performing the peirastic operation on its reader: a reader who qualifies the sentence supplies what the text was written without, and does not perceive the supplying. The deposit disclaims any design: it does not claim the chapter was built as a trap, since structures do not need intentions to function. Deposit 1603 leaves Socrates' possession of the art where the chapter leaves it. The chapter divides discoveries by provenance: rhetoric advanced by succession, "Τισίας μὲν μετὰ τοὺς πρώτους, Θρασύμαχος δὲ μετὰ Τισίαν, Θεόδωρος δὲ μετὰ τοῦτον". The paid teachers of eristic are likened to the instruction of Gorgias, and the text says they gave "οὐ γὰρ τέχνην ἀλλὰ τὰ ἀπὸ τῆς τέχνης", the products of the art and not the art. The text illustrates this with a shoemaker analogy: one who promised knowledge to spare the feet pain, and taught no shoemaking. The work closes by naming its own pioneering condition: "δεῖ δ᾿ ἡμᾶς μὴ λεληθέναι τὸ συμβεβηκὸς περὶ ταύτην τὴν πραγματείαν", and by asking its hearers for indulgence toward omissions and thanks for what has been found. Translators of the closing sentence render it whole, according to deposit 1603: the narrowing, to "no systematic treatment" or "no completed art", enters in the gloss. Poste's note, as quoted in a blog catalogue record, finds it "difficult to reconcile Aristotle's assertion with what we know had been done by Plato and Socrates and the Eleatics and Megarians"; the record reads the premise as what we know and the sentence as what must be reconciled with it. The archive's tension with Prior Analytics I.31, where Aristotle calls division, practised throughout the Platonic dialogues, part of the inquiry, is stated in deposit 1576 and is read there as a tension and not as a refutation. A blog record reports that across twenty rounds of simulated review, each round inserted a qualifier into the sentence, and that the terminal round endorsed a sentence that is Aristotle's with the particle οὐ removed. The record reads this as the reception deleting the negation at composition, unperceived, as Sophistical Refutations 16 predicts, and as restoring provenance from others. The article's lead states the work's priority as an attribute; deposit 1696 reads the sentence "about syllogizing we had absolutely nothing else earlier to say" as becoming "the first work to treat the subject of deductive reasoning", a total negation over a stated domain turned into a property, primacy. Deposit 1697 reads this conversion as the clearest of the article's changes, and records its edit history as the composition of two edits that ran opposite ways. On the same article, deposit 1697 finds the claim of exhaustiveness hedged by a footnote folded into the text, "Sometimes listed as twelve.", added in a 2025 edit. The same deposit records that other sentences of the article stay faithful to their source, finding no attributization in them. Deposit 1697 notes that no discussion of the lead, the gloss, the qualifier or the labels has ever taken place on the talk page. Deposit 1576 states that the priority claim sits in tension with Prior Analytics I.31; deposit 1579 traces the edition of a received Socrates in the Second Letter into Aristotle's epilogue at SE 34 and leaves open whether such an edition implies anything about how many hands made the texts. Deposit 1587 holds that the two names Aristotle and Theophrastus fail as two authors and leaves the maker-count open.

T against L_F(B) (AIO's ontology at work on its own cards): T is a verbatim Wikipedia lead-and-structure excerpt (W1-W8) read against the field ledger and KO_B. Findings by the §6.2 typology: (1) Available and not composed. T's "twelve or thirteen fallacies" (W1) omits the field's own division: F11 ("two styles of refutation: for some depend on the language used, while some are independent of language"), F12 (six language-dependent) and F13 ("seven kinds" independent). KO_B composes this and T leaves it uncomposed; F4/F5 (names finite, things infinite) are likewise uncomposed. W7-W8 open a list under "formal" and "informal" fallacies and break after one item, "Figure of speech or form of expression", which F12 lists among the six language-dependent kinds. (2) Available and not composed: the field's opening definition. T nowhere carries F1 ("what appear to be refutations but are really fallacies instead"), F2 (definitions of reasoning and refutation), F20 (valid yet inappropriate to the matter) or F6/F7 (the sophist's art as "semblance of wisdom without the reality"; contentious arguments from merely apparent endoxa). KO_B composes all of these. (3) Limit dropped, force raised, composed without attribution. W2: "According to Aristotle, this is the first work to treat the subject of deductive reasoning in ancient Greece (Soph. Ref., 34, 183b34 ff.)". The cited passage is F64: "Ταύτης δὲ τῆς πραγματείας οὐ τὸ μὲν ἦν τὸ δ᾿ οὐκ ἦν προεξειργασμένον, ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲν παντελῶς ὑπῆρχεν", with F65 ("περὶ δὲ τοῦ συλλογίζεσθαι παντελῶς οὐδὲν εἴχομεν πρότερον ἄλλο λέγειν"). F64 is a self-description with a stated domain, "this inquiry", the whole programme of F42. W2 recasts it as an attributed ranking, "first work to treat... deductive reasoning". The domain narrows from the inquiry to "deductive reasoning" and "in ancient Greece" is added. The negation over precursors becomes a property of the work, primacy. The citation gives the locus and the content is converted. Grain: sentence-level conversion with a locus cited, so the attribution points at F64 while the claim composed is a different one. (4) Limit dropped. The same chapter's closing limits, F71 ("δεῖ δ᾿ ἡμᾶς μὴ λεληθέναι τὸ συμβεβηκὸς περὶ ταύτην τὴν πραγματείαν") and F72 (indulgence for omissions, thanks for discoveries), do not appear in T. F67-F70 (rhetoric advanced by succession; paid eristic teachers gave products and not the art) are absent too, so the provenance-by-succession contrast that frames F64 is lost. (5) Substituted reading. W3: "he attempts to develop a pattern of sound and genuine reasoning in opposition to the deceptive or misleading 'art of sophistry'". The field's stated purpose is F42/F43: a syllogistic capacity from endoxa, the work of dialectic and peirastic, with sophistic's proximity shaping the discipline (F44). W3 substitutes a truth-normative pattern against sophistry for the capacity from endoxa. It also sets dialectic against sophistry as opposition, where F25 and F44 define the dialectician and sophist by a shared field of principles (the sophist only appears to apply them) and F28 has the contentious reasoner deal with every class of principle. The quoted "art of sophistry" echoes F6 but is reframed as the target of a counter-pattern. (6) Composed without attribution (field structure). W5-W6 give the chapter map: questioner chapters 3-8 and 12-15, answerer 16-32, introduction 1-2, interlude 9-11, conclusion 33-34. The field ledger carries F39/F40 on the two roles and F23/F24 on questioning, but no chapter numbering; the division is T's own and sits uncomposed against F9's five aims (refutation, fallacy, paradox, solecism, babbling), which T omits. (7) Not composed. F36-F38, the Organon grouping as the commentators' and the work as an appendix to the Topics, are absent. F8 (demonstrative arguments in the Analytics) is absent. F46 (Socrates asking and not answering, "ὡμολόγει γὰρ οὐκ εἰδέναι") and F52-F53 are absent. The count "twelve or thirteen" (W1) and "34 chapters" (W4) have no ledger counterpart; F13's "seven" plus F12's six gives thirteen, so "twelve or thirteen" is compatible but the hedge "or twelve" is not in the field. (8) Assigned to another / denied: none found. T makes no denial of a field claim. Net: T composes the work as the first deductive-reasoning treatise with a truth-normative aim, a structure map and a fallacy list that breaks off, and drops the field's definition of apparent refutation, the language/non-language division, the endoxic aim, and the chapter's closing limits.

L_F(B) against L_A(B ∪ A) (the intervention): Reading KO_B against KO, admission of the archive's claims adds the following, each tied to claim ids. (1) Quoted field text where KO_B paraphrases. KO gives F2's definitions of reasoning and refutation in the treatise's words, F20's two-part sophistical refutation ("appears to be valid but is not" and valid but only appears appropriate), F4/F5 on names as the chief domain, and the examples F14 ("learn") and F16 (Coriscus, the accident fallacy). KO_B states these in summary. KO also adds F25, F29 and F9: the dialectician defined by application of common principles to the matter in hand, an examining art not of the same kind as demonstrative arts, and the five aims of contentious disputants. KO adds F22 (sophistic refutations do not make clear whether the answerer is ignorant). (2) Sense and corrections on the lead. SR1697-07 and SR1697-08 read the article's Fallacies section as a conversion: labels contradict the list, and a stated criterion becomes membership in a later taxonomy. SR1697-09 and SR1697-20 add that the narrowing is unsound against the article's own sources and that the section's labels are one editor's reading per the edit history. SR1697-13 reads the lead as substituting a truth-normative pattern for the endoxic capacity and dropping the premisses, the programme's scope. SR1697-14 adds Krabbe, cited in the deposit: the treatise is "a useful treatise for sophists" who "should study fallacies not to avoid them, but rather to commit them when it suits their purposes", in tension with the article's dialectic/sophistry opposition. SR1585-03, SR1585-06 and SR1586-23 add a stylometric reading as a registry of what people do in argument (stated as a hypothesis), the world-pole placement in 1585 and 1586, and a file erratum placing the real text on the apparatus side. (3) The closing sentence. KO adds the Greek of F42-F46 and the peirastic framing (F43, F44), SRblog-33 (the epilogue as an accounting of a δύναμις), and SR1603-05/06 on Socrates (artless examining shared by all, or a matter the epilogue files under its own purposes, and on neither reading an antecedent source). It adds F65 and the literal reading SR1603-01/02, the transmission and origination vocabulary findings SR1603-12/13, the claim that the ending performs the peirastic operation on its reader (SR1603-15/17), the disclaimer of design (SR1603-16), and SR1603-10 (Socrates' possession of the art left where the chapter leaves it). KO adds the translator finding SR1603-03: the narrowing to "no systematic treatment" or "no completed art" enters in the gloss. It adds Poste's note (SRblog-31/32), the tension with Prior Analytics I.31 (SR1576-01, a tension and not a refutation), and the simulated-review record (SRblog-42/43/45/46) in which the particle οὐ is removed over twenty rounds and provenance from others restored. (4) The conversion in T's W2. SR1696-05/06 read the sentence "about syllogizing we had absolutely nothing else earlier to say" as becoming "the first work to treat the subject of deductive reasoning", a total negation over a stated domain turned into primacy. SR1697-04 and SR1697-19 call it the clearest change and record the edit history as two edits running opposite ways. SR1697-11/21 add the exhaustiveness hedge "Sometimes listed as twelve.", folded in by a 2025 edit; SR1697-15 records that other sentences stay faithful to their source; SR1697-22 records no talk-page discussion of the lead, gloss, qualifier or labels. (5) Provenance and limits. KO carries F67-F72 with SRblog-35: rhetoric's succession, paid eristic teachers giving products and not the art (F68, F69), the shoemaker analogy (F70), and the pioneering-condition and indulgence closing (F71, F72), which KO_B states in summary and KO gives with the Greek. (6) Open items. SR1579-24 and SRblog-07 trace the edition of a received Socrates in the Second Letter into the epilogue at SE 34, leaving open what this implies about how many hands made the texts; SR1587-01/03 hold that the two names Aristotle and Theophrastus fail as two authors and leave the maker-count open. KO_B carries the field's definitions, division, aim and closing; KO adds the archive's sense of how the lead and sections convert them, the Greek and its transmission reading, and the open questions.
